section: method: the f and g operators
text: The whole scheme is packaged as two conjugate autograd functions placed around each block ( Figure 3 ): Operator Where Forward pass Backward pass Why f block input identity all-reduce of the gradient every GPU needs the full X , and each contributes part of the gradient with respect to X , which must be summed g block output all-reduce identity sums the row-parallel partials Y i B i ; its gradient is already complete on every GPU Each is a few lines of PyTorch.
label: core

section: method: the f and g operators
text: The paper prints f ( Code 1 ); g swaps the two methods: class f(torch.autograd.Function): def forward(ctx, x): return x def backward(ctx, gradient): all_reduce(gradient) return gradient With one g and one f per block and two blocks per layer, a transformer layer needs exactly 4 all-reduces in total : 2 in the forward pass (one g per block) and 2 in the backward pass (one f per block), covering both attention and the MLP ( §3 , Figure 4 ).
label: core

section: method: duplicate cheap work rather than communicate
text: LayerNorm, dropout and the residual connections are cheap, so instead of one GPU computing them and broadcasting the result, every GPU keeps a duplicate copy of the LayerNorm parameters and runs dropout and the residual on the output of the parallel region before feeding the next one.
